This manuscript will likely be seen as a landmark contribution to the ever-improving understanding of the remarkably complex system of regulated membrane fusion.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Dissection of Synaptotagmin-1-SNARE complex interactions in solution and on membranes" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by Olga Boudker as the Senior Editor, a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Angel Perez Lara (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers and I have discussed the reviews with one another and I as Reviewing Editor have drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

As the editors have judged that your manuscript is of interest, but as described below that additional experiments are required before it is published, we would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). First, because many researchers have temporarily lost access to the labs, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts. We are also offering, if you choose, to post the manuscript to bioRxiv (if it is not already there) along with this decision letter and a formal designation that the manuscript is 'in revision at eLife'. Please let us know if you would like to pursue this option. (If your work is more suitable for medRxiv, you will need to post the preprint yourself, as the mechanisms for us to do so are still in development.)

All three reviewers and I agree that your paper is a very good eLife candidate. Our consensus is that your work represents a strong addition to our understanding of the synaptic vesicle fusion process by describing important aspects of the functional interplay between SNAREs, membranes, synaptotagmin, and complexin.

At the same time, the reviewers commented on a series of issues that we think need to be dealt with before your work can be published in eLife. The corresponding comments concern a set of more conceptual, interpretational, and methodological aspects, which can mostly be dealt with by careful revision of the manuscript text (A below), and include suggestions for a set of additional experiments and data analyses that we think are needed to support some of the key conclusions (B below).

Essential Revisions:

A) Conceptual, Interpretational, and Methodological Aspects:

i) While Zhou et al., (2017) used Cpx1-1-83 (crystallography) and Cpx1-48-73 (ITC), the present study employed Cpx1-26-83. This issue needs to be discussed as it may be problematic to compare characteristics of complexes formed with these different Cpx1 constructs. In essence it is possible that the type of Cpx1 fragment contributes to the relative stability and dynamics of the tripartite versus primary interface. Unless comparative experiments with exactly the same constructs are done, it is difficult to resolve discrepancies between the present and previous studies.

ii) Related to the point above (i), the 'assault' on the tripartite complex published by Zhou et al., (2017) appears overdone in some places and not always fully supported by the data. Zhou et al., (2017) really only observed the impact of the tripartite perturbations (LLQQ mainly) when they mutated away the primary interface using the quintuple C2B and quintuple SNAP25. In the present study the equivalent experiment was not done, and different protein fragments were used, so it is not clear if similar observations would have been made with NMR if exactly the same conditions/fragments would have been used. This issue should be taken into account when discussing the study by Zhou et al., (2017).

iii) The present study claims that LLQQ destabilizes Syt1, which then explains the published impact of this variant on synaptic transmission. This should be documented in the evidence as it is a crucial and impactful finding.

iv) Solution-state NMR is closer to physiologically significant conditions than crystallography. However, there are still major unresolved discrepancies between the present data and the ITC data of Zhou et al., (2017), where the experimental conditions are more comparable. In view of this and some other aspects, the 'physiological accuracy' of the experimental conditions in the present study appears oversold.

v) The discussion of the nanodisc-based data should consider the fact that clusters of SNAREs or Syt1 cannot form under these conditions even though these clusters do/may exist under physiological conditions and thus impose specific constraints on the prefusion complex and its relative stability. In essence, there is a possibility that physiologically important complexes are missed in the nanodisc scenario.

vi) In the study by Zhou et al., (2015), the destruction of the primary interface eliminated Syt1 function for both Ca2+-triggered fusion and inhibition of spontaneous release (clamping function), while the REKE and EAYW both strongly impaired Ca2+-triggered fusion without disrupting clamping. These perturbations occur on opposite sides of the β sandwich pointing in opposite directions and yet they cause very similar phenotypes at the synapse. Do both perturbations stabilize the primary interface at the expense of some other competitive interaction required for breaking the clamp upon Ca2+ binding? Or is there another interface not utilized during clamping but important for fusion that both these regions could contribute to? None of the three model interfaces (polybasic, primary, tripartite) simultaneously incorporate the RK and EY residue pairs at a shared interface. The authors of the present study should elaborate on the effects of REKE and EAYW in this context, perhaps by clarifying their own thinking on the issue.

B) Additional Data Analyses and Experiments:

i) The interpretation of NMR results is based on crystal structures. ITC experiments indicate a SNARE:C2B ratio of 2:1 – thus some of the results could be explained by cooperativity effects instead of competition between different binding sites. This should be analysed/discussed.

ii) In order to properly compare the Syt1 RQRQ, REKE, KEKE, and REKERQRQ variants, cooperativity factors need to be determined in order to assess the contribution of SNARE binding vs. membrane binding. Corresponding analyses of the WT, REKE, and RQRQ variants would suffice.

iii) To distinguish effects of variants on SNARE vs. membrane binding, additional experiments in the absence of anionic phospholipids are important. For instance, SNAP-25 could be used to monitor Syt11 C2AB binding (RQRQ, REKE, KEKE and REKERQRQ) to SNAREs using nanodisc with or without PS and PIP2, and with and without calcium. This would provide insight into the relative contribution of SNARE binding vs. membrane binding. Corresponding analyses of the WT, REKE, and RQRQ variants would suffice.

iv) Cooperativity factors (KD cisSC-ND/KD ND, KD cisSC-ND/KD cisSC-ND, KD ND/KD ND ratios) in the presence and absence of ATP/magnesium need to be determined, compared, and discussed.

Reviewer #1:

I continue to be enthusiastic about this manuscript, which I think is substantially above the bar for publishing in eLife. For reference, I am including below my original, positive review (slightly edited).

This manuscript represents a strong addition to our understanding of the functional interplay between SNAREs, membranes, synaptotagmin and, to a somewhat lesser extent perhaps, complexin. The authors have performed extensive NMR and fluorescence-based binding experiments with wild-type and informative mutant proteins, both in soluble form and (for the SNAREs) embedded in nanodiscs of various compositions. Although at first I found the sheer length of the manuscript daunting, I became convinced as I read it that the length is justified by the wealth of data and the need to carefully integrate the results with the extensive existing literature. I think the authors have succeeded to an impressive degree, and that this manuscript will be seen as a landmark contribution to our ever-improving understanding of this remarkably complex system.

There are many, many interesting results, but I would point single out three as deserving of special mention:

1. The striking differences, in vivo and in vitro, between two different double mutants (R322E/K325E versus K324E/K326E) in the same portion of synaptotagmin's polybasic region. The former has a much stronger effect that the latter on both PIP2-dependent membrane binding (this work) and neurotransmitter release (Brewer 2015). This can be beautifully reconciled by a detailed consideration of how the calcium-binding loops and the polybasic region cooperate in membrane binding of Ca2+-bound synaptotagmin (see Fig. 10B) and thereby promote fusion.

2. The remarkable finding that the E295A/Y338W mutation in the primary interface, previously claimed to abrogate synaptotagmin-SNARE binding (Zhou 2015), actually strengthens it. Given that this mutation compromises neurotransmitter release, the results highlight that overly avid binding can be as deleterious as compromised binding in vivo. I'm not sure why the Brunger lab reached the opposite conclusion about the impact of this double mutation on in vitro binding (Zhou 2015), but I found the results presented here to be convincing.

3. The strong implication that the tripartite SNARE:synaptotagmin:complexin interface, which was the main point of the Brunger lab's Nature paper and supported by ITC analysis of wild-type and mutant proteins (Zhou 2017), is a nonetheless a crystallization artifact, possibly induced by the artificial tether used in that work to link synaptotagmin to the SNARE bundle. Further work is underway, in collaboration with the Brunger lab, to resolve the contradiction, but my hunch is that the tripartite interface may not actually be physiologically important.

This manuscript represents an enormous amount of careful work, complemented by a highly intelligent and generally quite balanced synthesis of previous data from the author's and other labs. As such, I believe that it will be viewed as essential reading for anyone interested in the question of how, at a molecular mechanistic level, synaptic vesicles fuse in response to calcium.

Reviewer #2:

The authors have addressed my main concerns. They have carried out the requested experiments in order to clarify and support their conclusions. They have re-analyzed the results and re-written the manuscript regarding to the new data analysis and results. However, I still have one major concern:

I agree with authors that the stoichiometry for the binding of the SNARE complex to the C2B domain has not been reported but, as we can see in figure 3 b and d from Zhou Q et al., ITC results suggest a number of binding site (N) around 0.5 , what means 2 SNARE complex: 1 C2B domain stoichiometry. Additionally, this binding mode was suggested in the Extended Data Figure 9 of the same paper. Furthermore, ITC results argue against 1 C2B domain per SNARE complex, taking into account that the plateau starts around 1 molar ratio.

The authors claim "... that there is an interplay between binding of CpxSC to the primary interface and to the polybasic region. CpxSC appears to bind exclusively to one or the other site at low concentrations, likely because of steric hindrance disfavors simultaneous binding of two CpxSC complexes to one C2B domain. However, simultaneous binding to both sites might be allowed at higher CpxSC concentrations by slight alterations in both binding modes, leading to the curved cross-peak movement.'

I have some concerns about this issue. Taking into account the design of the ITC experiment (see above), at the very beginning we would get 2:1 stoichiometry for binding of the SNARE complex to the C2B domain because of there is a high concentration of complex against the low concentration of C2 domain. However, as we are injecting C2 domain, in a competition scenario, the experiment should present a number of binding site of 1 instead around 0.5, because of the increase of the C2 domain concentration will decrease the CpxSC:C2 domain ratio and , as consequence, several C2 domains will be accessible for competition per CpxSC complex. In addition, we can observe a chemical shift at low concentrations in the polybasic region (K327, K369 and K325) in the EAYW mutant (Fig. 4 C of the manuscript). Could it be possible a scenario in which two CpxSC complexes bind to 1 C2 domain ( even at low concentration of CpxSC complex) and the different mutations tune the interplay of the polybasic region and primary interface ( maybe even promoting different binding modes), giving the observed NMR results? We have to take into account that the binding is dynamic (as reported previously Brewer et al., 2015).

Despite of the above comments, I am aware of the effort carried out by the authors and in my opinion they addressed my main concerns and I suggest and support the publication of the manuscript in eLife.

Reviewer #3:

The authors have dealt with my major scientific concerns (comparisons of identical CPX constructs with Brunger lab results) and clarified their conclusions/interpretations of the EAYW vs REKE mutations. They have also convincingly demonstrated that the tripartite binding mode does not contribute to SNARE interactions under their experimental conditions while also toning down their conclusion that the tripartite mode is entirely a crystal artifact. I agree with the authors that the specific Brunger lab comparisons should be published separately and in coordination with that lab rather than included here. The edits made the manuscript a bit easier to read and I appreciate the authors trying to limit the amount of new data included to avoid expanding the text/figures even more. The discussion section is still quite hefty, and I would recommend some more editing for clarity, but this is a minor issue. Overall, this is an impressive amount of data and the conclusions contain some important new insights. I support going forward with publication.

claims.claim: The affinity of C2AB* for cisSC-NDs and transSC-NDs is similar.
claims.source: Titrations of C2AB* with transSC-NDs and cisSC-NDs yielded similar results (Figure 5D) and comparable apparent KDs (118 nM and 96 nM, respectively).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The FRET efficiencies observed at saturating concentrations are consistent with the binding modes involving the polybasic region and the primary interface.
claims.source: The FRET efficiencies are consistent with the binding modes involving the polybasic region and the primary interface, which predict that the probe on C2AB* is located at comparable, short distances from residues 34 and 76, and farther from residues 16, but are not consistent with the tripartite complex, where residue 346 of C2AB* is expected to be much closer to residue 16 than to residue 76 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on FRET data in Figure 5E and distance calculations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Complexin-1 does not substantially alter the interaction of C2AB* with the nanodisc-anchored SNARE complex.
claims.source: We also analyzed the effect of including complexin-1 on binding of C2AB* to cisSC-NDs labeled at residue 34 of SNAP-25 and observed similar binding curves and apparent KDs (Figure 5F; Supplementary file 1), suggesting that complexin-1 does not substantially alter the interaction of C2AB* with the nanodisc-anchored SNARE complex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: There is a strong synergy between binding of Ca2+-free C2AB* to the SNARE complex and the nanodisc phospholipids.
claims.source: These results suggest that there is a strong synergy between binding of Ca2+-free C2AB* to the SNARE complex and the nanodisc phospholipids.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on FRET data showing much higher affinity for cisSC-NDs than NDs in the absence of Ca2+ (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: PIP2 enhances binding of the C2B domain to membranes due to interactions with the polybasic region.
claims.source: Since PIP2 enhances binding of the C2B domain to membranes due to interactions with the polybasic region (Bai et al., 2004; Li et al., 2006), we performed titrations with NDs and cisSC NDs containing 1% PIP2 and indeed observed much higher affinities at 50 mM KCl (Figure 5G, black and red curves; apparent KDs 286 nM and 43 nM, respectively).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2004; Li et al., 2006 and FRET data in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The increases in affinity caused by simultaneous binding of C2AB* to the nanodiscs and the SNARE complex were considerably lower in the presence than in the absence of Ca2+, particularly when the nanodiscs contained PIP2.
claims.source: Overall, the increases in affinity caused by simultaneous binding of C2AB* to the nanodiscs and the SNARE complex were considerably lower in the presence than in the absence of Ca2+, particularly when the nanodiscs contained PIP2 (Supplementary file 1, 2).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of cooperativity factors calculated from the FRET data (Supplementary files 1-2).

claims.claim: Mutations in the polybasic region impair Ca2+-independent binding to PIP2-containing NDs much more strongly than the R398Q/R399Q mutation.
claims.source: Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to NDs was markedly impaired by all mutations, but mutations in the polybasic region impaired binding to NDs containing PIP2 much more strongly than the R398Q/R399Q mutation (Figure 6A,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claims.claim: Binding of C2AB* to PIP2-containing NDs is mediated largely by the polybasic region.
claims.source: Hence, binding to these nanodiscs is mediated largely by the polybasic region, as expected, but the tandem arginines also participate in binding to some extent.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of mutations on binding to PIP2-containing NDs (Figure 6A,C).

claims.claim: Both the tandem arginines (R398,R399) and the polybasic region are important for Ca2+-independent, simultaneous binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex and the lipids.
claims.source: Thus, both the tandem arginines (R398,R399) and the polybasic region are important for Ca2+-independent, simultaneous binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex and the lipids.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data showing that mutations in both regions impair binding to cisSC-NDs (Figure 6B,D).

claims.claim: The underlying Ca2+-independent interactions are dynamic and involve at least two binding modes whereby either the primary interface or the polybasic region interacts with the SNAREs.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the underlying interactions are dynamic and involve at least two binding modes whereby either the primary interface containing R398,R399 or the polybasic region interacts with the SNAREs and the other basic sequence (the polybasic region or R398,R399) binds to the lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mutation data and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: The R322E/K325E mutation impairs Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing NDs much more dramatically than the K324E/K326E mutation.
claims.source: Importantly, the R322E/K325E mutation impaired Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing NDs much more dramatically than the K324E/K326E mutation (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 6A; apparent KDs 49–62 nM for the K324E/K326E mutant and 1.5–2.9 μM for R322E/K325E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 6A.

claims.claim: There is a specific Ca2+-dependent binding mode of Syt1 to PIP2-containing membranes that involves R322,K325 but not K324,K326.
claims.source: These findings show that there is a specific Ca2+-dependent binding mode of Syt1 to PIP2-containing membranes that involves R322,K325 but not K324,K326, and suggest that the specific, strong disruption of neurotransmitter release induced by the R322E/K325E mutation but not the K324E/K326E mutation arises from impairment of Ca2+-dependent binding of Syt1 to the (PIP2-containing) plasma membrane rather than to the SNARE complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of the mutations on Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing NDs.

claims.claim: The specific, strong disruption of neurotransmitter release induced by the R322E/K325E mutation arises from impairment of Ca2+-dependent binding of Syt1 to the PIP2-containing plasma membrane rather than to the SNARE complex.
claims.source: These findings show that there is a specific Ca2+-dependent binding mode of Syt1 to PIP2-containing membranes that involves R322,K325 but not K324,K326, and suggest that the specific, strong disruption of neurotransmitter release induced by the R322E/K325E mutation but not the K324E/K326E mutation arises from impairment of Ca2+-dependent binding of Syt1 to the (PIP2-containing) plasma membrane rather than to the SNARE complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between the biochemical data and physiological effects.

claims.claim: Interactions of C2AB* with the SNARE complex contributed much less to binding to cisSC-NDs in the presence of Ca2+ than in its absence.
claims.source: The cooperativity factors calculated from KD NDs/KD cisSC-NDs in the presence of Ca2+ under various conditions (Figure 6E–H, Figure 6—figure supplements 4–6) ranged from 1.39 to 3.11 and hence were considerably smaller than those observed in EGTA (Supplementary file 2), indicating that interactions of WT C2AB* with the SNARE complex contributed much less to binding to cisSC-NDs in the presence of Ca2+ than in its absence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of cooperativity factors from the FRET data (Supplementary file 2).

claims.claim: Ca2+-dependent interactions of C2AB* with PIP2 on the nanodiscs preclude interactions with the SNARE complex.
claims.source: Interestingly, the cooperativity factors observed for WT C2AB* in the presence of PIP2 were particularly small, suggesting that Ca2+-dependent interactions of C2AB* with PIP2 on the nanodiscs preclude interactions with the SNARE complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the small cooperativity factors observed in the presence of Ca2+ and PIP2.

claims.claim: Ca2+ induces binding of the C2B domain in an approximately perpendicular orientation to the membrane that favors insertion of both Ca2+-binding loops into the bilayer.
claims.source: Because Ca2+ induces binding of the C2B domain in an approximately perpendicular orientation to the membrane that favors insertion of both Ca2+-binding loops into the bilayer (Araç et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2004; Rufener et al., 2005), this orientation allows binding of R322 and K325 to PIP2, but K324 and K326 point away from the membrane because they are on the opposite side of the same β-strand (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; see also Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2004; Rufener et al., 2005 and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and Figure 10B.

claims.claim: In the perpendicular orientation induced by Ca2+, interaction of the SNARE complex with the primary interface of the C2B domain is impossible because it would place the syntaxin-1 C-terminus far from the membrane where it is anchored.
claims.source: In this configuration, interaction of the SNARE complex with the primary interface of the C2B domain is impossible because it would place the syntaxin-1 C-terminus far from the membrane where it is anchored (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Simultaneous Ca2+-dependent binding of the C2B domain to the membrane through its Ca2+-binding loops and to the SNARE complex through its polybasic region is in principle compatible with anchoring of syntaxin-1 to the membrane.
claims.source: Simultaneous Ca2+-dependent binding of the C2B domain to the membrane through its Ca2+-binding loops and to the SNARE complex through its polybasic region is in principle compatible with anchoring of syntaxin-1 to the membrane (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), but this binding mode is expected to be prevented by PIP2 because PIP2 binds to K322,R325, the same residues of the polybasic region that are key for SNARE complex binding (Brewer et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and prior data from Brewer et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB* to PIP2-containing membranes is incompatible with the two major Syt1-SNARE complex binding modes, which involve the primary and polybasic interfaces.
claims.source: In summary, Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB* to PIP2-containing membranes is incompatible with the two major Syt1-SNARE complex binding modes, which involve the primary and polybasic interfaces.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRET data and modeling.

claims.claim: Upon Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent membrane binding, R398 and R399 can still be involved in non-specific interactions with negative residues of the SNARE complex.
claims.source: However, upon Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent membrane binding, R398 and R399 can still be involved in non-specific interactions with negative residues of the SNARE complex, and such interactions are also possible if the C2B domain binds in a more slanted orientation to membranes lacking PIP2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F.

claims.claim: The E295A/Y338W mutation did not alter binding to NDs under various conditions.
claims.source: Interestingly, this mutation did not alter binding to NDs under various conditions (Figure 7) but caused a considerable increase in affinity for cisSC-NDs containing 15% PS and 1% PIP2 in the absence of Ca2+, compared to WT C2AB* (Figure 7A; apparent KDs 366 nM for WT C2AB* and 80 nM for the E295A/Y338W mutant).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The E295A/Y338W mutation enhances Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex within cisSC-NDs via the primary interface.
claims.source: The results obtained in the absence of Ca2+ correlate with the increased affinity of the Syt1 C2B domain for CpxSC observed in our NMR experiments (Figure 4) and show that this mutations enhances Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex within cisSC-NDs via the primary interface.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data in Figure 7A and NMR data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The lack of an overt effect of the E295A/Y338W mutation on binding to cisSC-NDs in the presence of Ca2+ strongly supports the notion that the primary interface is not involved in Ca2+-dependent binding.
claims.source: However, the lack of an overt effect of the E295A/Y338W mutation on binding to cisSC-NDs in the presence of Ca2+ strongly supports the notion that the primary interface is not involved in Ca2+-dependent binding.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on FRET data in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: C2AB* binds more strongly to cisSC-PC-NDs than to solubleSC in the absence of Ca2+.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+, C2AB* bound more strongly to cisSC-PC-NDs than to solubleSC (KD 0.93 and 5.5 μM, respectively), and binding to cisSC-PC/PS/PIP2-NDs was even tighter (KD0.49 μM) (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Interactions of both the polybasic region and R398,R399 with the lipids contribute to Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to cisSC-NDs.
claims.source: These findings are fully consistent with the conclusion that interactions of both the polybasic region and R398,R399 with the lipids contribute to Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to cisSC-NDs, and hence that such binding involves at least two types of interactions where either the primary interface binds to the SNAREs and the polybasic region to the lipids, or the polybasic region binds to the SNAREs and R398,R339 to the lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data in Figure 8 and modeling in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Even interactions of C2AB* basic residues with neutral phospholipids such as PC can enhance binding to the SNARE complex.
claims.source: As expected, the PC/PS/PIP2-NDs enhanced binding to the SNARE complex more than the PC-NDs, but it is noteworthy that even interactions of C2AB* basic residues with neutral phospholipids such as PC can enhance binding to the SNARE complex.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on FRET data comparing binding to PC-NDs vs PC/PS/PIP2-NDs (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB* to PIP2-containing membranes is incompatible with SNARE complex binding through the primary and polybasic interfaces.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the notion that Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB* to PIP2-containing membranes is incompatible with SNARE complex binding through the primary and polybasic interfaces.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data showing low FRET efficiencies for binding to cisSC-PC/PS/PIP2-NDs in the presence of Ca2+ (Figure 8H).

claims.claim: Non-specific interactions of R398,R399 of WT C2AB* with acidic residues from the SNAREs may facilitate binding to the SNARE-containing side of nanodiscs.
claims.source: Non-specific interactions of R398,R399 of WT C2AB* with acidic residues from the SNAREs may facilitate binding to the SNARE-containing side (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E), leading to some FRET, but mutation of these arginines may lead to preferential binding of the R398Q/R399Q mutant to the other side, particularly at high nanodisc concentrations when membrane availability is not limiting.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation to explain the bimodal binding curve observed for the R398Q/R399Q mutant (Figure 8H).

claims.claim: Ca2+-independent binding of WT C2AB* to the SNARE complex persists in the presence of Mg-ATP.
claims.source: These results suggested that Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex persists in the presence of Mg-ATP, but Ca2+-dependent binding is strongly impaired.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex is strongly impaired in the presence of Mg-ATP.
claims.source: These results suggested that Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB* to the SNARE complex persists in the presence of Mg-ATP, but Ca2+-dependent binding is strongly impaired.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In the presence of Mg-ATP, Ca2+-independent binding of WT C2AB* to the SNARE complex on nanodiscs involves at least two binding modes mediated by either the primary or the polybasic interface.
claims.source: These results suggest that, in the presence of Mg-ATP, Ca2+-independent binding of WT C2AB* to the SNARE complex on nanodiscs also involves at least two binding modes mediated by either the primary or the polybasic interface, and the former is stabilized by the E295A/Y338W mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRET data showing effects of mutations on binding in the presence of Mg-ATP (Figure 9C-D).

claims.claim: The R322E/K325E mutation disrupts Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing NDs much more strongly than the K324E/K326E mutation in the presence of Mg-ATP.
claims.source: We also verified that the R322E/K325E mutation disrupts Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing NDs much more strongly than the K324E/K326E mutation in the presence of Mg-ATP (Figure 9F), confirming the specificity of such impairment under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: Syt1 binds to the SNARE complex before Ca2+ influx, most likely through the primary interface.
claims.source: Together with available data, the study presented here suggests that Syt1 binds to the SNARE complex before Ca2+ influx, most likely through the primary interface, and that Ca2+ actually releases this interaction, inducing tight membrane binding that involves specific interactions of the C2B polybasic region with PIP2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Ca2+ releases the Syt1-SNARE complex interaction, inducing tight membrane binding that involves specific interactions of the C2B polybasic region with PIP2.
claims.source: Together with available data, the study presented here suggests that Syt1 binds to the SNARE complex before Ca2+ influx, most likely through the primary interface, and that Ca2+ actually releases this interaction, inducing tight membrane binding that involves specific interactions of the C2B polybasic region with PIP2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The Syt1-SNARE complex keeps the release machinery in a state that hinders membrane fusion but at the same time is ready for fast release when Ca2+ induces binding of the Syt1 Ca2+-binding loops to the membrane.
claims.source: We propose that the Syt1-SNARE complex keeps the release machinery in a state that hinders membrane fusion but at the same time is ready for fast release when Ca2+ induces binding of the Syt1 Ca2+-binding loops to the membrane, releasing the Syt1-SNARE interaction and enabling cooperation between Syt1 and the SNAREs in membrane fusion (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The mechanism of action of Syt1 remains enigmatic, in part because dozens of papers have described Syt1-SNARE interactions but it is unclear which of these interactions is physiologically relevant.
claims.source: While these ideas are attractive, the mechanism of action of Syt1 remains enigmatic, in part because dozens of papers have described Syt1-SNARE interactions but it is unclear which of these interactions is physiologically relevant and which ones arise merely from the high promiscuity of these proteins (Jahn and Scheller, 2006; Rizo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citations to Jahn and Scheller, 2006; Rizo et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The functional importance of binding of Syt1 to the SNARE complex through the primary interface is overwhelmingly supported by physiological data.
claims.source: The functional importance of binding of Syt1 to the SNARE complex through the primary interface is overwhelmingly supported by physiological data (Guan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015.

claims.claim: High PIP2 concentration should favor simultaneous binding of the C2B domain polybasic region to this lipid and of the primary interface to the SNARE complex.
claims.source: For instance, our experiments used 1% PIP2, which corresponds to the average PIP2 content of the plasma membrane, but clusters containing 6% PIP2 have been detected (James et al., 2008; van den Bogaart et al., 2011). High PIP2 concentration should favor simultaneous binding of the C2B domain polybasic region to this lipid and of the primary interface to the SNARE complex (Figure 10A,C).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the known existence of PIP2 clusters (James et al., 2008; van den Bogaart et al., 2011) and modeling shown in Figure 10A,C.

claims.claim: A cryo-EM structure revealed a slanted orientation of the SNARE complex that should hinder full zippering at the C-terminus and was disrupted by Ca2+.
claims.source: Such a state has been observed by cryo-EM on lipid nanotubes, albeit at limited resolution (Grushin et al., 2019). The structure revealed a slanted orientation of the SNARE complex that should hinder full zippering at the C-terminus and was disrupted by Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grushin et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Even if the SNARE complex is less slanted in the primed state, a more parallel orientation of the SNARE complex with respect to the membrane would still hinder C-terminal zippering, which could explain the increase in spontaneous release observed in Syt1 KO mice.
claims.source: Even if the SNARE complex is less slanted in the primed state, a more parallel orientation of the SNARE complex with respect to the membrane (e.g. Figure 10A) would still hinder C-terminal zippering, which could explain the increase in spontaneous release observed in Syt1 KO mice (Xu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on modeling (Figure 10A) and a citation to Xu et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The proposed state is consistent with the observation that complexin-1 does not alter the affinity of C2AB* for cisSC-NDs.
claims.source: The proposed state is also consistent with the observation that complexin-1 does not alter the affinity of C2AB* for cisSC-NDs (Figure 9E), as complexin-1 and Syt1 bind to opposite sides of the SNARE complex (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on FRET data in Figure 9E and the model in Figure 10A.

claims.claim: In the proposed state, the helix formed by complexin-1 would point toward the vesicle membrane, also hindering SNARE complex zippering.
claims.source: In this state, the helix formed by complexin-1 would point toward the vesicle membrane (Figure 10A,C), also hindering SNARE complex zippering (Trimbuch et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the model shown in Figure 10A,C and a citation to Trimbuch et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The proposed model provides a basis for the findings that complexin-1 is required for the dominant negative effect of Syt1 bearing mutations in the C2B domain Ca2+-binding sites.
claims.source: This model provides a basis for the findings that complexin-1 is required for the dominant negative effect of Syt1 bearing mutations in the C2B domain Ca2+-binding sites (Zhou et al., 2017) and that Syt1 is necessary for the inhibition of spontaneous release by complexin in Drosophila (Jorquera et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed model and citations to Zhou et al., 2017 and Jorquera et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The R398Q/R399Q mutation strongly disrupts binding of the C2B domain to the SNARE complex through the primary interface.
claims.source: Our finding that the R398Q/R399Q mutation strongly disrupts binding of the C2B domain to the SNARE complex through the primary interface (Figure 2B,C) suggests that such disruption underlies the dramatic impairment of Ca2+-evoked neurotransmitter release caused by this mutation, as well as the abrogation of clamping of spontaneous release by Syt1 (Xue et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR data in Figure 2B,C and citations to Xue et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The E295A/Y338W mutation enhances (rather than weakens) Ca2+-independent binding of Syt1 to the SNARE complex.
claims.source: These findings are readily explained by our model and our biochemical data, as the E295A/Y338W enhances (rather than weakens) Ca2+-independent binding of Syt1 to the SNARE complex (Figures 4, 7A, 8 and 9D) and hence hinders release of the inhibitory Syt1-SNARE interaction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on data presented in Figures 4, 7A, 8 and 9D.

claims.claim: The R322E/K325E mutation impairs Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent membrane binding, which is critical to release the inhibitory Syt1-SNARE interaction.
claims.source: Similarly, the R322E/K325E mutation impairs Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent membrane binding, which is critical to release this inhibitory interaction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRET data showing impaired Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing membranes (Figures 6G and 9F).

claims.claim: The available data support the notion that, before Ca2+ influx, the trans-SNARE complex, complexin-1 and Syt1 form a macromolecular assembly between the vesicle and plasma membranes that inhibits release but is ready to trigger fast membrane fusion upon Ca2+ influx.
claims.source: Altogether, the available data support the notion that, before Ca2+ influx, the trans-SNARE complex, complexin-1 and Syt1 form a macromolecular assembly between the vesicle and plasma membranes that inhibits release but is ready to trigger fast membrane fusion upon Ca2+ influx because it brings Syt1 close to the SNAREs (Figure 10C left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: The Syt1 C2 domains bridge the vesicle and plasma membranes upon Ca2+ influx.
claims.source: In this model, Ca2+ triggers tight, specific binding of the C2B domain to PIP2 and other lipids in the plasma membrane while binding of C2B to the SNARE complex is released. The mechanisms underlying the last events leading to membrane fusion are still unclear, but we speculate that the Syt1 C2 domains bridge the vesicle and plasma membranes (Araç et al., 2006; Figure 10C, middle panel).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on prior data (Araç et al., 2006) and illustrated in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: Insertion of the C2 domain Ca2+-binding loops into the membrane can induce membrane curvature to facilitate membrane fusion.
claims.source: This action could cooperate with the SNAREs in bringing the membranes together, and insertion of the C2 domain Ca2+-binding loops into the membrane can induce membrane curvature (Martens et al., 2007) to facilitate membrane fusion (Figure 10C, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on a citation to Martens et al., 2007 and illustrated in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: R398,R399 are critical for the membrane-membrane bridging activity of Syt1.
claims.source: Note that R398,R399 are critical for the membrane-membrane bridging activity of Syt1 and therefore the strong disruption of neurotransmitter release caused by mutating these arginines might arise from impairment of this activity (Araç et al., 2006; Xue et al., 2008) in addition to abrogating SNARE binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2006; Xue et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The strong disruption of neurotransmitter release caused by mutating R398,R399 might arise from impairment of the membrane-membrane bridging activity in addition to abrogating SNARE binding.
claims.source: Note that R398,R399 are critical for the membrane-membrane bridging activity of Syt1 and therefore the strong disruption of neurotransmitter release caused by mutating these arginines might arise from impairment of this activity (Araç et al., 2006; Xue et al., 2008) in addition to abrogating SNARE binding.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the known functions of R398,R399.

claims.claim: Syntaxin-1 is known to form clusters on the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Thus, syntaxin-1 is known to form clusters on the plasma membrane (Khuong et al., 2013), and formation of Syt1 oligomers has been proposed to underlie the primed state and to exert an inhibitory activity that is released by Ca2+ (Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khuong et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Formation of Syt1 oligomers has been proposed to underlie the primed state and to exert an inhibitory activity that is released by Ca2+.
claims.source: Thus, syntaxin-1 is known to form clusters on the plasma membrane (Khuong et al., 2013), and formation of Syt1 oligomers has been proposed to underlie the primed state and to exert an inhibitory activity that is released by Ca2+ (Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The Syt1 oligomers are compatible with the state proposed in Figure 10A.
claims.source: However, the Syt1 oligomers are compatible with the state proposed in Figure 10A (Tagliatti et al., 2020) and hence can be readily incorporated into the model of Figure 10C.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tagliatti et al., 2020.

results.result: NMR spectroscopy reveals that the Syt1 C2B domain binds to the complexin-1-SNARE complex (CpxSC) through both the polybasic region and the primary interface in solution with similar affinities (KD > 20 μM), and Ca2+ does not affect the binding mode.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C56, C72, and C73 are directly supported by NMR data presented in Figures 1H-K showing chemical shift perturbations in both the polybasic region and primary interface upon CpxSC titration. The similar affinities and Ca2+-independence are demonstrated by comparable cross-peak shifts in both Ca2+-free and Ca2+-bound conditions (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

results.result: The R398Q/R399Q mutation strongly disrupts binding of the C2B domain to the SNARE complex through the primary interface both in solution and on nanodiscs, which underlies the dramatic impairment of neurotransmitter release caused by this mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C60, C76, C77, and C130 are well-supported by NMR data (Figure 2B,C) showing abolished cross-peak shifts at the primary interface and FRET data (Figures 6-9) demonstrating impaired binding to cisSC-NDs. The correlation with physiological effects is supported by citations to prior studies (Xue et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2015).

results.result: The E295A/Y338W mutation enhances (rather than weakens) Ca2+-independent binding of Syt1 to the SNARE complex both in solution and on nanodiscs, which explains the impairment of neurotransmitter release by hindering release of the inhibitory Syt1-SNARE interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C61, C83, C108, and C131 are supported by NMR data (Figure 4) showing increased cross-peak shifts and FRET data (Figures 7A, 8, 9D) demonstrating enhanced binding affinity. The paradoxical effect—enhanced binding yet impaired release—is logically explained by the proposed model where stronger binding prevents Ca2+-induced release of the inhibitory interaction.

results.result: Binding of the C2B domain to CpxSC through the tripartite interface could not be detected by NMR even after abolishing interactions through the polybasic region and primary interface with the quadruple R322E/K325E/R398Q/R399Q mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C78, and C79 are supported by NMR data (Figures 2E, 3) showing no cross-peak shifts or intensity changes for the quadruple mutant even at 85 μM CpxSC. This directly contradicts prior ITC data (Zhou et al., 2017) and suggests the tripartite interface observed crystallographically may be a crystal contact artifact.

results.result: Ca2+-free synaptotagmin-1 C2AB binds to SNARE complexes anchored on nanodiscs with strong synergy between SNARE complex and lipid interactions, as demonstrated by much higher affinity for cisSC-NDs than for NDs lacking SNARE complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C58, C85, C86, and C90 are supported by FRET data (Figure 5C) showing apparent KD of 26.6 nM for cisSC-NDs versus 129.5 nM for NDs in the presence of Ca2+, and even larger differences in the absence of Ca2+ (141 nM vs 8.7 μM). The cooperativity factors calculated from these data (Supplementary files 1-2) quantitatively demonstrate the synergy.

results.result: Ca2+ induces tight binding of synaptotagmin-1 to PIP2-containing nanodiscs and disrupts synaptotagmin-1-SNARE interactions, as evidenced by dramatically reduced cooperativity factors in the presence of Ca2+ and PIP2.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C92, C100, C101, and C120 are supported by FRET data showing cooperativity factors ranging from 1.39 to 3.11 in the presence of Ca2+ compared to 6.64 to 62.1 in EGTA (Supplementary file 2). The particularly small cooperativity factors with PIP2 suggest Ca2+-dependent C2AB*-PIP2 interactions preclude SNARE complex binding.

results.result: The R322E/K325E mutation disrupts Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing membranes much more strongly than the K324E/K326E mutation (KD 1.5-2.9 μM vs 49-62 nM), correlating with their differential effects on neurotransmitter release and indicating that the specific disruption arises from impaired Ca2+-dependent binding to the plasma membrane rather than to the SNARE complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C65, C66, C97, C98, C99, and C118 are strongly supported by FRET data (Figures 6G, 9F) showing the dramatic differential effect of these mutations on Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing NDs. The correlation with physiological effects (Brewer et al., 2015) and the specificity of this effect only in the presence of Ca2+ and PIP2 provide compelling evidence for the interpretation.

results.result: In the presence of Mg-ATP, Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB to SNARE complexes anchored on PIP2-nanodiscs is almost abolished, but Ca2+-independent binding persists.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C64, C115, and C116 are supported by FRET data (Figure 9A,B, Figure 9—figure supplements 1-2) showing that Mg-ATP dramatically reduces the difference in FRET between cisSC-NDs and NDs in the presence of Ca2+ but not in EGTA. This reconciles conflicting prior reports (Park et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016) by showing Ca2+-dependent binding is abolished while Ca2+-independent binding remains.

results.result: The data suggest a model where synaptotagmin-1 binds to the SNARE complex through the primary interface before Ca2+ influx, forming a macromolecular assembly that inhibits release but is ready for fast membrane fusion when Ca2+ releases this interaction and induces tight PIP2/membrane binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C12, C119, C120, C121, and C133 represent the central mechanistic model supported by the collective data: NMR showing primary interface binding in solution, FRET showing Ca2+-independent binding to membrane-anchored SNARE complexes, and Ca2+-induced disruption of this interaction with concomitant tight PIP2 binding. The model is illustrated in Figure 10 and integrates all major findings.

results.result: Ca2+-independent binding of C2AB to cisSC-NDs involves dynamic interactions with at least two binding modes where either the primary interface or the polybasic region interacts with the SNAREs while the other basic sequence binds to lipids.
results.evaluation: Claims C93, C94, C95, C96, and C111 are supported by FRET data (Figures 6A-D, 8) showing that mutations in both the polybasic region and R398,R399 impair Ca2+-independent binding to cisSC-NDs, with differential effects on binding to NDs versus cisSC-NDs. The modeling in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B illustrates how these two binding modes could occur.

results.result: Ca2+ induces binding of the C2B domain in an approximately perpendicular orientation to the membrane that allows R322 and K325 to bind PIP2, but this orientation is incompatible with the primary and polybasic SNARE complex binding modes because it would place the syntaxin-1 C-terminus far from the membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C103, C104, and C105 are supported by structural modeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D, Figure 10B) based on prior structural studies (Araç et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2004; Rufener et al., 2005) and the FRET data showing incompatibility of Ca2+-dependent PIP2 binding with SNARE complex interactions. The perpendicular orientation explains the differential effects of R322E/K325E versus K324E/K326E mutations.

results.result: Complexin-1 does not substantially alter the affinity of C2AB for membrane-anchored SNARE complexes, consistent with the proposed model where complexin-1 and Syt1 bind to opposite sides of the SNARE complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C89, and C127 are supported by FRET data (Figures 5F, 9E) showing similar binding curves and apparent KDs with or without complexin-1. This is consistent with the structural model (Figure 10A) where complexin-1 binds to the opposite side of the SNARE complex from the Syt1 primary interface.

results.result: Including the complexin-1 fragment Cpx1(26-83) dramatically improved the solubility of mixtures containing the Ca2+-bound C2B domain and the SNARE complex, enabling NMR analysis without KSCN.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C70, and C71 are supported by UV spectroscopy data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing reduced precipitation with Cpx1(26-83) and the observation that Syt1 C2 domains do not bind to complexin-1 under the NMR conditions. This methodological advance enabled the key NMR experiments.

results.result: The R322E/K325E mutation abolishes binding of CpxSC to the polybasic region and reveals that the polybasic region not only competes with the primary interface for binding to CpxSC but also hinders full C2B-SNARE engagement at the primary interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 are supported by NMR data (Figure 2A,C,D) showing no shift in the K369 cross-peak (polybasic region) but more extensive shifts at the primary interface for the R322E/K325E mutant compared to WT. This suggests the polybasic region sterically hinders optimal primary interface binding.

results.result: The L387Q/L394Q mutation causes considerable destabilization of the Syt1 C2B domain, suggesting that the disruption of neurotransmitter release caused by this mutation may have arisen from general loss of function due to protein instability rather than specific disruption of the tripartite interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C82 are supported by NMR data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing broad cross-peaks characteristic of protein instability and sample precipitation upon CpxSC addition, consistent with the 10°C decrease in thermal denaturation temperature reported by Zhou et al., 2017. This provides an alternative explanation for the physiological effects of this mutation.

results.result: The affinity of C2AB* for cisSC-NDs and transSC-NDs is similar (apparent KDs 96 nM and 118 nM), and the FRET efficiencies at saturating concentrations are consistent with binding modes involving the polybasic region and primary interface but not the tripartite complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C87 and C88 are supported by FRET data (Figure 5D,E) showing comparable binding curves and KDs for cis and trans SNARE complexes. The FRET efficiency analysis with probes at different SNAP-25 positions (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) supports the polybasic/primary interface binding modes over the tripartite interface.

results.result: The E295A/Y338W mutation did not alter binding to NDs under various conditions but enhanced Ca2+-independent binding to cisSC-NDs, while having no overt effect on Ca2+-dependent binding to cisSC-NDs, strongly supporting that the primary interface is not involved in Ca2+-dependent binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C107 and C109 are supported by FRET data (Figure 7) showing no effect on ND binding, enhanced binding to cisSC-NDs in EGTA (KD 80 nM vs 366 nM for WT), but minimal effect in Ca2+. This differential effect provides strong evidence that the primary interface mediates Ca2+-independent but not Ca2+-dependent SNARE binding.

results.result: C2AB* binds more strongly to cisSC-PC-NDs than to soluble SNARE complex in the absence of Ca2+ (KD 0.93 μM vs 5.5 μM), and even interactions with neutral phospholipids such as PC can enhance binding to the SNARE complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C110 and C112 are supported by FRET data (Figure 8A) showing tighter binding to cisSC-PC-NDs than soluble SNARE complex. The observation that even PC-only nanodiscs enhance SNARE binding demonstrates that electrostatic interactions with acidic lipids are not absolutely required for the synergy between lipid and SNARE binding.

results.result: In the presence of Mg-ATP, Ca2+-independent binding of WT C2AB* to the SNARE complex on nanodiscs involves at least two binding modes mediated by either the primary or the polybasic interface, with the former stabilized by the E295A/Y338W mutation.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by FRET data (Figure 9C-D) showing that in the presence of Mg-ATP, the E295A/Y338W mutation enhances binding to cisSC-NDs while other mutations impair it, similar to the pattern observed without ATP. This demonstrates that the same binding modes persist under physiological ATP conditions.

results.result: Prior physiological studies showed that R398Q/R399Q and E295A/Y338W mutations at the primary interface strongly impair neurotransmitter release, and that R322E/K325E but not K324E/K326E mutations in the polybasic region disrupt release.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C5, C34, C35, and C38 are supported by citations to prior physiological studies (Xue et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2015; Brewer et al., 2015). These established physiological effects provide the functional context for interpreting the biochemical data in this study.

results.result: Three structures of Syt1-SNARE complexes have been determined showing drastically different binding modes: NMR revealed a dynamic interaction involving the polybasic region, X-ray crystallography revealed a primary interface involving E295/Y338 and R398/R399, and a tripartite structure showed an α-helix of C2B continuing the complexin-1 helix.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C31, C32, C33, C36, C37, C41, and C42 accurately describe prior structural studies (Brewer et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017) as illustrated in Figure 1A-G. These prior structures provide the structural framework for the current study's investigation of which binding modes are physiologically relevant.

results.result: Prior studies showed that Syt1-SNARE co-immunoprecipitation was not significantly altered by the R398Q/R399Q mutation and only moderately disrupted by the E295A/Y338W mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 are supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2015. The discrepancy between these co-IP results and the strong binding disruption observed by NMR in the current study is explained by the authors as potentially arising from co-IP detecting polybasic region binding upon membrane solubilization and depending on off-rates as well as affinities.

results.result: Prior ITC studies suggested the existence of a tripartite Syt1-complexin-1-SNARE complex interaction and that the dominant negative effect of Syt1 C2B Ca2+-binding site mutations requires complexin-1, with the L387Q/L394Q mutation disrupting binding and impairing release.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, C45, C46, and C80 describe prior results from Zhou et al., 2017 that conflict with the current NMR data showing no tripartite interface binding. The authors note they are collaborating with the Brunger lab to resolve this discrepancy, and the current study suggests the L387Q/L394Q effects may arise from protein destabilization rather than specific interface disruption.

results.result: A genetic screen in Drosophila for mutations that abrogate the dominant negative effect of Syt1 C2B Ca2+-binding site mutations yielded many mutations in the primary interface but none in the tripartite interface, suggesting the dominant negative effect requires binding through the primary rather than tripartite interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C49 are supported by citation to Guan et al., 2017. This genetic evidence supports the physiological relevance of the primary interface over the tripartite interface, consistent with the current study's findings.

results.result: Prior studies reported conflicting results on Ca2+ effects on Syt1-SNARE binding: many studies showed Ca2+ strongly stimulates binding, the Ca2+-binding loops are not involved in the three Syt1-SNARE structures, Ca2+ disrupted Syt1-SNARE complexes on lipid tubes, and ATP was reported to abolish Syt1-SNARE binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C51, C52, C53, C54, and C55 accurately summarize the confusing and contradictory state of the literature regarding Ca2+ effects on Syt1-SNARE interactions, supported by multiple citations. The current study aims to resolve these contradictions.

results.result: The introduction provides established background on neurotransmitter release, including the roles of SNAREs, Munc18-1, Munc13s, NSF, SNAPs, and synaptotagmin-1 structure and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C29 represent well-established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide the scientific context for the study but do not represent new findings.

results.result: The mechanism of action of Syt1 remains enigmatic due to dozens of papers describing Syt1-SNARE interactions of unclear physiological relevance, though the functional importance of the primary interface is overwhelmingly supported by physiological data.
results.evaluation: Claims C122 and C123 accurately characterize the state of the field and are supported by citations (Jahn and Scheller, 2006; Rizo et al., 2006; Guan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015). This provides the rationale for the current study's systematic investigation.

results.result: High PIP2 concentration in clusters should favor simultaneous binding of the C2B polybasic region to PIP2 and the primary interface to the SNARE complex, and a cryo-EM structure revealed a slanted SNARE complex orientation that should hinder C-terminal zippering and was disrupted by Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C124, C125, and C126 involve speculation about PIP2 clusters (supported by citations to James et al., 2008; van den Bogaart et al., 2011) and interpretation of a low-resolution cryo-EM structure (Grushin et al., 2019). While plausible, these claims involve significant inference beyond the direct data and the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether the cryo-EM orientation was dictated by helical packing.

results.result: In the proposed state, the complexin-1 helix would point toward the vesicle membrane and hinder SNARE complex zippering, providing a basis for findings that complexin-1 is required for the dominant negative effect of Syt1 C2B Ca2+-binding site mutations and that Syt1 is necessary for complexin inhibition of spontaneous release.
results.evaluation: Claims C128 and C129 are supported by the structural model (Figure 10A,C) and citations to prior physiological studies (Trimbuch et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017; Jorquera et al., 2012). The model provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for these prior observations.

results.result: The R322E/K325E mutation impairs Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent membrane binding, which is critical to release the inhibitory Syt1-SNARE interaction.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 is supported by FRET data (Figures 6G, 9F) showing strong impairment of Ca2+-dependent binding to PIP2-containing membranes by the R322E/K325E mutation. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the physiological effects of this mutation.

results.result: The proposed model speculates that Syt1 C2 domains bridge the vesicle and plasma membranes upon Ca2+ influx, with insertion of Ca2+-binding loops inducing membrane curvature to facilitate fusion, and that R398,R399 are critical for this membrane-bridging activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C134, C135, C136, and C137 represent speculative elements of the proposed model (Figure 10C) based on prior data (Araç et al., 2006; Martens et al., 2007; Xue et al., 2008). While plausible and consistent with prior findings, these mechanistic details of the fusion process are not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Syntaxin-1 forms clusters on the plasma membrane and Syt1 oligomers have been proposed to underlie the primed state, and these oligomers are compatible with the proposed state and can be incorporated into the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C138, C139, and C140 are supported by citations to prior studies (Khuong et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017; Tagliatti et al., 2020). The authors note these features can be incorporated into their model, though they were not directly investigated in the current study.

results.result: The primary interface is involved in binding to the nanodisc-anchored SNARE complex.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is a conclusion drawn from the mutation data showing that R398Q/R399Q impairs and E295A/Y338W enhances binding to cisSC-NDs both in solution and on nanodiscs. This conclusion is well-supported by the collective data from Figures 2, 4, 6-9.

results.result: PIP2 enhances binding of the C2B domain to membranes due to interactions with the polybasic region.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by citations to prior studies (Bai et al., 2004; Li et al., 2006) and FRET data in the current study (Figure 5G) showing much higher affinities for PIP2-containing NDs. This represents established knowledge confirmed by the current data.

results.result: Upon Ca2+- and PIP2-dependent membrane binding, R398 and R399 can still be involved in non-specific interactions with negative residues of the SNARE complex, which may facilitate binding to the SNARE-containing side of nanodiscs.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C114 represent speculation based on modeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F) to explain residual FRET and bimodal binding curves observed for some mutants (Figure 8H). While plausible, these non-specific interactions are not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Ca2+-dependent binding of C2AB* to PIP2-containing membranes is incompatible with SNARE complex binding through the primary and polybasic interfaces.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by FRET data (Figure 8H) showing low FRET efficiencies (0.4) for binding to cisSC-PC/PS/PIP2-NDs in the presence of Ca2+, in contrast to high FRET efficiencies (>0.7) observed under other conditions. This is consistent with the structural modeling showing incompatibility.

results.result: KSCN might have favored binding of the SNARE complex to the C2B domain polybasic region over the primary interface, and the increased affinity caused by the E295A/Y338W mutation may arise from replacing tyrosine with tryptophan.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C84 represent speculation about potential mechanisms. While plausible, these mechanistic explanations are not directly tested and represent hypotheses for future investigation.
